content: Phlegm is a viscous fluid secreted by the mucous membranes of animals. Its definition is specifically limited to the mucus produced by the respiratory system, excluding that from the nasal passages, and particularly refers to the mucus expelled through coughing, known as sputum. The composition of phlegm varies depending on factors such as climate, genetics, and the state of the immune system. However, it is fundamentally a water-based gel that contains glycoproteins, immunoglobulins, lipids, and other components. In the context of Hippocratic medicine, phlegm was historically considered one of the four bodily humors, alongside blood, black bile, and yellow bile. It was thought to possess the qualities of coldness and wetness and was associated with apathetic and sluggish behavior. This ancient belief is preserved in the term phlegmatic, which describes a calm or unemotional temperament. Phlegm can present in various colors, each of which may indicate different physiological or pathological conditions: Clear or white phlegm is generally considered healthy and normal. Yellow phlegm often signifies an infection. During the early stages of a common flu, when the phlegm is still clear, the individual is most infectious. As the phlegm turns yellow, it indicates that the body is actively combating the infection. Greenish or brownish phlegm is almost always a sign of infection. Greenish or rusty-colored phlegm, or phlegm with rusty spots, may also indicate pneumonia or internal micro-bleeding. Brown phlegm is commonly associated with smoking. This occurs due to the adhesion of tar and resin to the viscous texture of the phlegm, which is then expelled by the body. Brownish-gray phlegm, another type often linked to smoking, is encased in clear saliva. When spread out, the brown-gray core appears grainy in texture, as opposed to cohesive. This variant may consist of dust and other foreign particles and is often associated with damage to the cilia, as seen in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Phlegm can also be a carrier of larvae from intestinal parasites, such as hookworms. The presence of blood in sputum, known as hemoptysis, can be a symptom of serious diseases like tuberculosis or lung cancer. However, it may also be a relatively benign symptom of minor conditions such as bronchitis, in which the sputum is typically streaked lightly with blood. Coughing up significant amounts of blood is always a serious medical condition and requires immediate medical attention. In some cases, blood in phlegm may result from a nosebleed, where blood has traveled down the throat and mixed with mucus. The concept of phlegm also has historical significance in the theory of humorism. Humorism posits that the human body is composed of four fundamental substances, known as the four humors, which must remain in balance for a person to maintain health. An excess or deficiency in any of these humors was believed to cause disease or disability. The four humors—black bile, yellow bile, phlegm, and blood—were thought to correspond to the four classical elements of earth, fire, water, and air, respectively.
